title: It's time to make friends
author: Josue Valles
summary: Josue Valles argues that in an age when AI gives everyone the same leverage, the durable advantage for professionals is a trusted personal network rather than an audience. He traces how mass media, the internet and social media let people trade trust for familiarity at scale, and says AI pushes that logic to the limit so that knowledge and attention both become cheap. Because opportunities still move through people, who you know now matters more than what you know. He uses the farmer metaphor of cultivating relationships before you need them, draws on Granovetter's strength of weak ties to explain why acquaintances open more doors than close friends, and distinguishes vertical relationships with clients from horizontal ones with connectors. His practical method is content-led networking: using podcasts, interviews and small studies to start real conversations, and planting seeds by giving value first. The essay carries a promotional note for a paid workshop, but the argument itself is substantive.
points: When AI makes knowledge and posting nearly free, trust becomes the scarce asset and attention matters only as the front door to it.
Opportunities are a lagging indicator: the ones you receive this year come from relationships planted years earlier, so cultivate them before you are hungry.
Moderately weak ties, people who remember you but do not share your circle, produce more opportunities than close friends, so build many acquaintances in different places.
Treat content as a relationship tool by interviewing people you admire and measuring success by how many conversations continue, not by downloads.
Make yourself easy to describe in one sentence, since acquaintances can only pass your name along if they can say who you help and how.
quotes: Opportunities move through people. Every time you want a better job, new clients, capital, a spouse, a second chance, you need a human being on the other side of the door to open it for you.
The problem is that the promise of AI is universal. If you don’t need anyone’s permission, neither does anyone else.
In times of universal leverage, who you know becomes more important than what you know.
A farmer can’t make a seed grow faster by pulling on it. They prepare the soil, plant, water, pull weeds and wait.
What this means is that you probably need more acquaintances than you think, and you need them in different places.
An audience gives you visibility. It’s one person talking to many, and the relationship only goes one way: you talk, and they listen.
The scarcest asset is trust, not attention. The only reason attention matters is that it’s the front door to trust.
A close friend could explain your work in detail. An acquaintance only has what you’ve made obvious.
